query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling and low‐temperature thermal exposure, differences in atomic size and self‐diffusion rates among Cr, Co, Fe, Ni, and Al lead to local elemental segregation from the high‐temperature homogeneous BCC state in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7. The ensuing lattice strain and elastic stresses lower the stability of the BCC phase and promote its decomposition into ordered secondary phases (for example, sigma or B2), whereas rapid quenching suppresses these segregation‐driven transformations.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a homogenized, high-temperature BCC supersaturated solid solution.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled cooling protocols and subsequent annealing treatments at, e.g., 600°C or 900°C, while comparing with samples that are rapidly quenched from the high-temperature state.
generation.conditions: This mechanism should operate when the cooling rate and thermal exposure allow sufficient atomic mobility (i.e., under slow cooling or prolonged moderate annealing), but it should be suppressed by extremely rapid cooling or minimal hold times where diffusion is limited.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized elemental segregation and the resulting lattice strain fields that serve as nucleation sites for the emergence of secondary ordered phases.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in atomic radii and diffusion coefficients, slower cooling permits differential partitioning of elements. This leads to local segregation (for example, Cr- or Al-rich regions) and the buildup of internal elastic stresses. These stresses destabilize the single-phase BCC matrix, triggering a transformation (via nucleation and growth of precipitates) to equilibrium or metastable secondary phases such as sigma or B2, thereby relieving the accumulated strain.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to slow cooling and/or annealing will develop detectable secondary phases (as evidenced by additional XRD reflections, TEM features, or segregated compositions by EDS) and will typically show increased hardness due to the presence of precipitates or lattice strain relaxation. In contrast, samples that are rapidly quenched will largely retain the homogeneous BCC structure with minimal segregation.
generation.baseline: A rapidly quenched sample that retains a single-phase, homogeneous BCC structure with minimal evidence of element segregation and no formation of secondary phases.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected only when the thermal exposure (either via slow cooling or annealing) allows for significant diffusion; if cooling is too rapid or temperatures are too low for atomic migration, then the segregation and subsequent phase decomposition will not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise identity (e.g., sigma versus B2) and volume fraction of the resulting secondary phases, as well as the exact magnitude of the induced lattice strains, remain to be quantified. Subtle effects from minor compositional fluctuations could also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 specimens and subject them to two distinct thermal treatments: (1) rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state to lock in the homogeneous microstructure, and (2) slow cooling or isothermal annealing (e.g., at 600°C or 900°C) to allow for diffusion. Characterize the resulting samples via X-ray diffraction (to identify additional phase reflections), transmission electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (to map elemental segregation and secondary phase morphology), and microhardness measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled or annealed samples do not show any signs of secondary ordered phase formation or local elemental segregation—that is, if they remain structurally and compositionally identical to the rapidly quenched baseline with similar hardness—then the hypothesis that diffusion‐driven segregation and strain-induced phase decomposition governs the phase evolution is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Microstructure and phase composition of L-PBF sample are very similar to those of the powder. The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable. In the present study, the powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was synthesized via gas atomization and then used for laser powder bed fusion and microplasma spraying processes. Microstructure and phase composition stability were studied. FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 in equilibrium state consists of B2 and σ-phase. Gas atomization led to a formation of partially ordered BCC super saturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich and Al-rich segregations. The alloy remained single-phase after powder consolidation via laser powder bed fusion procedure. The non-equilibrium solid solution decomposes with B2 and σ-phase formation only after annealing at 900 °C for 1 h. Maximal microhardness (950 HV) was obtained for the powder and the L-PBF sample annealed at 600 °C, which is caused by increasing element segregation and growth of elastic stresses. After annealing at 900 °C microhardness slightly decreased (850 HV) but remained higher than that in the initial state, it is explained by from one hand stress relaxation, from other homogeneous precipitation of hard σ-phase.
